title: Debugging Coroutines & Coroutines vs Alternatives
scopeHtml: Scope: debug mode, coroutine naming, IDE debugger, DebugProbes, stack-trace recovery, leak hunting, coroutine overhead, and coroutines vs threads/Executors/callbacks/RxJava including migration and Rx-to-Flow mapping.

questions.promptHtml: What does the -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug flag do, and how would you use it on an Android project where you see log lines like Thread[DefaultDispatcher-worker-3] and cannot tell which coroutine is running?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you have ever actually debugged concurrent code instead of guessing, and whether you know debug facilities are opt-in and platform-dependent.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "It turns on kotlinx.coroutines debug mode. Every coroutine gets a unique id, and while a thread runs a coroutine, the library renames the thread to something like DefaultDispatcher-worker-3 @fetchUser#42. It also turns on stack-trace recovery. It is auto by default, which means on only when JVM assertions are enabled, so it is on in JVM unit tests but off in a normal Android app. On Android I flip it on in debug builds by setting the system property before any coroutine class loads."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Internally there is a top-level DEBUG flag read once, at class initialisation, from System.getProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug"). Values: on/empty string = on, off = off, auto (default when the property is absent) = on iff assertions are enabled (-ea). JVM tests run with -ea (Gradle test tasks enable assertions by default), so you get it free there. A release or debug Android app does not run with assertions, so the flag is off.

When it is on:

  1. Each coroutine created gets a sequential CoroutineId (a context element). toString() of a job shows "StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@1b2c3d"; with debug it also shows the name/id.
  2. While a continuation resumes, CoroutineScheduler/DispatchedContinuation wraps execution and temporarily sets Thread.currentThread().name to <original> @<CoroutineName>#<id>, restoring afterwards. That is what you see in logcat %t thread names and in a thread dump.
  3. Stack-trace recovery is enabled (see the stack-trace recovery question).

Because it is read once at class init, you must set it early:

Application.attachBaseContext / onCreate   (before the first coroutine builder is touched)
   System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on")   <- only if BuildConfig.DEBUG

Caveat: if any library already initialised the coroutines DebugKt class before your line runs, it is too late. Putting it in a ContentProvider/App Startup initializer or attachBaseContext is safer than onCreate. I would verify on the exact coroutines version with a one-line log of Thread.currentThread().name inside a launch.

Overhead: the doc describes it as negligible, but the thread rename allocates strings on every resume, so I keep it out of release builds and out of benchmark builds.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class App : Application() {
    override fun attachBaseContext(base: Context) {
        super.attachBaseContext(base)
        if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.debug", "on")
    }
}

fun log(msg: String) = println("[${Thread.currentThread().name}] $msg")

fun main() = runBlocking(CoroutineName("main")) {
    launch(Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineName("fetchUser")) { log("loading") }
    // with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug:
    // [DefaultDispatcher-worker-1 @fetchUser#2] loading
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting the property late (after coroutines classes loaded) and concluding "it does not work on Android".
  • Assuming the thread name is renamed without the flag. CoroutineName alone does not change the thread name; it only lives in the context.
  • Leaving debug mode on in a release build and then being surprised by extra string allocations.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it on in unit tests? → Yes via auto, because Gradle enables assertions for test JVMs.
  2. Does it need the kotlinx-coroutines-debug artifact? → No. The flag is in core. The artifact adds DebugProbes.
  3. Does it change behavior of my code? → Not semantically, but it enables stack-trace recovery, which can change the exception instance you catch (it is a copy with the original as cause).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Adds coroutine names to logs." Senior: explains auto vs on, that it is read once at class-init, why it is on in tests and off in apps, the Android bootstrap approach, and the stack-trace recovery side effect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team chasing a Dispatchers.IO starvation could not tell which feature was blocking threads; turning on debug mode in the QA build and reading thread names in an ANR trace pointed straight at the blocking coroutine.

questions.promptHtml: How do you make logs from concurrent coroutines traceable? Where does CoroutineName actually show up and where does it not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Distinguishes people who know CoroutineName is just a context element from those who think it magically appears everywhere.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "CoroutineName is a context element, so it is inherited by children and can be overridden with +. It is visible via coroutineContext[CoroutineName], in Job.toString(), in the diagnostic context attached to uncaught-exception reports, and in thread names only when debug mode is on. For logs I write a small helper that reads it from the context, or put a request id into MDC via asContextElement."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Context is a map keyed by CoroutineContext.Key. CoroutineName("x") has Key = CoroutineName. Rules:

  • Child inherits parent context, then its own argument overrides: launch(CoroutineName("child")) replaces the parent's name for that child and its subtree.
  • It does not touch threads unless debug mode is enabled.
  • withContext(CoroutineName("db")) { } renames for the block only.
  • Not available in non-suspending callbacks; you must capture it first.

Where it appears:

Place Shows name?
coroutineContext[CoroutineName]?.name Always
job.toString() Yes: "fetchUser#2":StandaloneCoroutine{Active}@.. in debug mode; name shown in recent versions via nameString()
Thread name Only with debug mode
Uncaught exception crash Recent versions (1.7+/1.8) add a suppressed DiagnosticCoroutineContextException carrying the context string, which includes the name. Verify on your version.
DebugProbes dump Yes
Plain Log.d No, you must add it

For structured correlation across layers (request id, user id), the right tool is a custom context element, or ThreadLocal.asContextElement(value) for MDC-like thread-locals so the value follows the coroutine across thread hops.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun tag(): String =
    coroutineContext[CoroutineName]?.name ?: "unnamed"

suspend fun logd(msg: String) = Log.d("App", "[${tag()}] $msg")

val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main + CoroutineName("CheckoutVM"))

scope.launch(CoroutineName("pay")) {
    logd("start")                     // [pay] start
    withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { logd("io") } // [pay] io (inherited)
}

val requestId = ThreadLocal<String>()
launch(requestId.asContextElement("req-91")) { /* thread-local follows hops */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting Log.d thread names to include the coroutine name without debug mode.
  • Naming only the scope and then wondering why every child shows the same name (children inherit; name per launch).
  • Using raw ThreadLocal across withContext hops and losing the value (needs asContextElement).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does + order matter? → For different keys no; for the same key the right side wins.
  2. Is CoroutineName propagated into flow {} collection? → Collector context is the upstream's flowOn context; the name of the collecting coroutine is visible in the collector, upstream gets what flowOn sets.
  3. How do you carry a trace id through coroutines to a backend call? → Custom AbstractCoroutineContextElement read in an OkHttp interceptor via a captured value, or asContextElement plus MDC; be careful that OkHttp interceptors run on OkHttp threads, so capture before the hop.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Name your coroutines for debugging." Senior: lists exactly where the name surfaces, ties it to debug mode, handles thread-local propagation, and builds a correlation id strategy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Crash reports said only IllegalStateException in DefaultDispatcher-worker-4; adding names to every top-level launch made the Crashlytics custom key identify the owning feature in minutes.

questions.promptHtml: What does the IDE coroutine debugger give you that a regular breakpoint and stack view does not, and how does it work given that a suspended coroutine has no thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand coroutines are heap objects (state machines) and how tooling reconstructs "virtual stacks".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A suspended coroutine is not on any thread stack, so the normal Frames view cannot show it. The Kotlin debugger plugin reads the continuation objects on the heap, using @DebugMetadata the compiler adds to each state-machine class, and rebuilds a virtual stack of suspend frames. The Coroutines tab lists all coroutines with state (running, suspended, created) and their async stack. It can also show the creation stack if creation tracking is enabled."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each suspend fun with suspension points compiles into a ContinuationImpl subclass holding a label (state number), spilled locals, and a completion reference to the caller's continuation. The completion chain is the logical call stack. The compiler annotates these classes with kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.DebugMetadata (source file, line numbers per label, spilled variable names, method name). The debugger walks completion chain and maps label to a line, giving frames like:

Coroutine "fetchUser#2" SUSPENDED
  at UserRepo.load(UserRepo.kt:41)
  at UserVM$refresh$1.invokeSuspend(UserVM.kt:27)

Features: view suspended coroutines, see variables spilled to the continuation, "Capture coroutine creation stack" option (async stack trace of where launch was called; implemented with the same agent mechanism as DebugProbes in the IDE-run JVM, with a performance cost), and a coroutine dump action. In Android Studio the Kotlin plugin offers the coroutine view during a debug session; I would confirm the exact feature set for the Studio version in use, since Android Studio lags IntelliJ.

Limits: optimised-away tail calls and inlined suspend lambdas can produce missing frames; ProGuard/R8 renaming affects metadata names in obfuscated builds (debug builds are fine); breakpoints inside a coroutine suspend the thread currently running it, not the whole scope, so other coroutines continue unless you set suspend-all.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun load(id: String): User {
    val raw = api.get(id)        // breakpoint here: Frames shows thread stack;
    return parse(raw)            // Coroutines tab shows suspended callers too
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Debugging with the thread dropdown only, then seeing an "empty" stack after a suspension point resumes on another thread.
  • Leaving creation-stack capture on during a performance investigation, skewing timings.
  • Expecting the coroutine tab to work for release/minified builds.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a stack look different before and after delay? → Resume happens from the dispatcher loop via resumeWith, not by returning through original frames; only the continuation chain preserves logical stack.
  2. What is the "Coroutine boundary" line in traces? → Marker inserted by stack-trace recovery separating the recovered frames from the original.
  3. How is this different from DebugProbes? → IDE uses the debugger/agent attached to the process; DebugProbes is a library API you call programmatically (JVM only, not Android runtime).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "There is a Coroutines tab." Senior: explains continuation chain, DebugMetadata, label-to-line mapping, creation-stack cost, and obfuscation limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An engineer debugging a "stuck loading spinner" found 14 coroutines all SUSPENDED on the same Mutex.lock in the tab, a view the thread stack could never provide.

questions.promptHtml: Why are coroutine stack traces often missing your call site, and what is stack-trace recovery? What does it change about exceptions you catch?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Signals depth on exception propagation and a classic "why is my catch type/identity weird" gotcha.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "When a coroutine resumes, the thread stack only has the dispatcher frames plus the current state-machine frame, not the original callers. Stack-trace recovery, enabled in debug mode, copies the exception when it crosses a suspension boundary, such as await(), and stitches the receiving coroutine's frames onto it, with the original as cause. So the exception you catch can be a different instance of the same class."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Throwing inside withContext(IO) { throw IOException() } creates a trace deep in worker frames. By the time await() or withContext rethrows in the caller's coroutine, the trace shows nothing about the caller. Recovery fixes that: in recoverStackTrace(exception, continuation) it reflectively creates a copy via a constructor (String, Throwable), (Throwable), (String), or no-arg, sets the stack to the caller frames from the continuation chain, a (Coroutine boundary) separator, then the original trace; the original exception becomes the cause.

Consequences:

  • e === originalException is false; e.cause === original.
  • Equality/when (e) on class still works if the copy keeps the class. Types with only unusual constructors are skipped (no copy) unless they implement StackTraceRecoverable.copyForStackTraceRecovery() (experimental, check opt-in).
  • Custom fields lost when copy uses (message) constructor only: data in extra properties may be missing on the copy. This bites custom exceptions with error codes.
  • Cost: reflection + stack building; that is why it is debug-only. Disable explicitly with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.stacktrace.recovery=false.
  • Exceptions that are CancellationException are handled too, and the trace appears in cancellation logs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ApiException(val code: Int, msg: String) : Exception(msg)

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val d = async(Dispatchers.Default) { throw ApiException(500, "boom") }
    try { d.await() } catch (e: ApiException) {
        // debug mode: e is a copy only if ctor shape matches; code may be lost
        println(e.cause)  // original, with its worker stack
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using identity comparison or storing exception instances in a map keyed by identity.
  • Assuming custom fields survive the copy.
  • Reading only the top trace and ignoring Caused by with the Coroutine boundary section.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does it run in release builds? → Not by default; it follows debug mode.
  2. How do you get a useful trace in production without it? → Wrap at boundaries with your own exception adding context, name coroutines, log breadcrumbs.
  3. Can it cause a test to behave differently from prod? → Yes: tests run with -ea so recovery is on; a test that asserts assertSame on exception fails, and the converse bug can hide.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Gives better traces." Senior: explains copy-with-cause mechanics, constructor requirements, lost custom fields, identity pitfalls, and test/prod divergence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A retry layer mapped ApiException.code to user messages; unit tests passed but a debug-mode QA build showed code 0 because the copy used the (message) constructor path.

questions.subtopic: Debugging a crash with an unhelpful trace
questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (1.2M DAU, Android 8-14, Pixel and Samsung mix) shows a new top crash after release 5.14 at 0.6% of sessions:

FATAL EXCEPTION: DefaultDispatcher-worker-2
java.lang.IllegalStateException: Cart item missing
    at com.shop.cart.CartMapper.map(CartMapper.kt:58)
    at com.shop.cart.CartRepo$load$2.invokeSuspend(CartRepo.kt:34)
    at kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith(ContinuationImpl.kt:33)
    at kotlinx.coroutines.DispatchedTask.run(DispatchedTask.kt:108)
    at kotlinx.coroutines.scheduling.CoroutineScheduler.runSafely(...)

Nothing shows which screen triggered it. The team has 40 launch calls in 12 view models. A background refresh and the checkout screen both call CartRepo.load.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find which caller produces the crash and what do you ship?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add try/catch in CartRepo and log." That hides the crash without identifying the caller and may swallow data errors. Or "reproduce locally" with no plan when it is 0.6% of sessions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did it start exactly at 5.14, so which change touched Cart? (narrows diff). Is it tied to a specific backend payload or locale? (data vs concurrency). Is there a CoroutineExceptionHandler or Crashlytics breadcrumbs already? Are crashes foreground or background session?
  2. Immediate mitigation: If it is data-dependent, a server-side or remote-config kill switch for the new mapper path; otherwise a staged rollout halt at 20 percent. Do not blindly catch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) malformed payload for a subset of carts, exception is legitimate; (b) race: background refresh mapping a stale snapshot while checkout mutates it; (c) mapper change in 5.14 mishandling a null field; (d) red herring: dispatcher thread, since worker-2 is just where it ran.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add CoroutineName per top-level launch and attach it to Crashlytics custom keys via a CoroutineExceptionHandler on the scope and via the DiagnosticCoroutineContextException suppressed entry; add a breadcrumb in CartRepo.load(caller). Check Crashlytics breakdown by app version, screen key, device. Replay the payload in a unit test.
  5. Root cause: Stack shows only the dispatcher; the logical call chain was lost at the thread hop. After tagging, 95 percent of crashes came from the background refresh worker mapping carts containing a delisted SKU the checkout path pre-filtered.
  6. Fix: Short-term: map delisted SKUs to a skipped item with a logged non-fatal. Long-term: make the mapper return Result/sealed type, fix at the boundary, and give every top-level scope a name plus handler:
class AppScope(name: String, crash: CrashReporter) {
    private val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { ctx, t ->
        crash.setKey("coroutine", ctx[CoroutineName]?.name ?: "unnamed")
        crash.record(t)
    }
    val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + CoroutineName(name) + handler)
}
  1. Prevention: Convention: every launch in a repository entry point is named; detekt rule against bare GlobalScope; debug builds with the debug flag on; test with the failing payload.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No blanket catch (Throwable): it also eats CancellationException. No permanent debug-mode in release.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Handler does not fire for the crash. → Exceptions in a child of a scope with a handler only reach it if it is the root coroutine or the handler is in context at root; a launch inside coroutineScope or async bypasses it.
  • Crash only on Samsung. → Probably data/locale or process-death timing rather than the dispatcher; segment before guessing.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a retail app: an anonymous "worker-N" crash was three different features sharing one repository. Two lines of naming and a Crashlytics key cut triage from two days to an hour.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Wraps in try/catch, no way to identify the caller.
  • Hire: Names coroutines, uses handler and breadcrumbs, segments by version.
  • Strong hire: Explains why the trace is lost, handler scoping rules, fixes the data contract, and adds prevention conventions.

questions.promptHtml: What is DebugProbes, what does dumpCoroutines() print, and can you use it on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you know the one tool that answers "what is every live coroutine doing right now".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "DebugProbes is in the kotlinx-coroutines-debug module. It installs a Byte Buddy-based agent that tracks every coroutine's creation and state, so dumpCoroutines() prints all live coroutines with their state and stack, and printScope/printJob show hierarchies. It is a JVM feature: the debug agent is not supported on Android runtime, so I use it in JVM unit tests and Robolectric, and in the IDE during debug sessions."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: DebugProbes.install() (or -javaagent:kotlinx-coroutines-debug-<ver>.jar; on newer JDKs the javaagent is preferred to avoid attach warnings) re-defines the stdlib's kotlin.coroutines.jvm.internal.DebugProbesKt class so probeCoroutineCreated/Resumed/Suspended hooks populate a registry of weak references to coroutines. Hence it sees every coroutine, including those with no strong reference.

Useful APIs:

  • DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines() prints Coroutine "name#id":StandaloneCoroutine{Active}, state: SUSPENDED plus the (sanitized) stack.
  • dumpCoroutinesInfo() returns CoroutineInfo list for programmatic assertions: state is CREATED, RUNNING or SUSPENDED.
  • jobToString(job), printJob(job), printScope(scope) for hierarchy.
  • enableCreationStackTraces (default true when installed; costly), sanitizeStackTraces (drop internal frames), ignoreCoroutinesWithEmptyContext.
  • @CoroutinesTimeout (JUnit 5) / CoroutinesTimeout.seconds() rule (JUnit 4): when a test hangs, dumps all coroutines then fails.

Android: Byte Buddy agent attach needs a JVM tooling interface that ART does not provide, so no. Also its transitive dependencies (JNA, Byte Buddy) can cause duplicate-resource packaging failures if added to the app module; keep it in testImplementation and exclude duplicate license files if the build complains.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build.gradle.kts: testImplementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-debug:<same as core>")
@CoroutinesTimeout(testTimeoutMs = 5_000)   // JUnit 5 extension
@Test fun `refresh finishes`() = runBlocking {
    DebugProbes.install()
    try {
        val job = launch { neverCompletes() }
        delay(100)
        DebugProbes.printJob(job)
    } finally { DebugProbes.uninstall() }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adding kotlinx-coroutines-debug as implementation in the app module and shipping Byte Buddy.
  • Calling install() and forgetting uninstall(), polluting later tests.
  • Using version mismatch between core and debug artifacts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do the dumps hold references without leaking? → Registry uses weak references.
  2. Can I query it in production? → Not on Android; for server JVMs you can install it, but disable creation stack traces for overhead.
  3. How do you find a hung runTest? → @CoroutinesTimeout or runTest timeout (default 60s in recent versions; confirm) plus the dump.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "A debug library for coroutines." Senior: knows agent mechanism, weak refs, Android non-support, packaging pitfall, timeout rule, and the programmatic dumpCoroutinesInfo for assertions.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky CI test hung forever once a month; @CoroutinesTimeout printed a coroutine suspended on a CompletableDeferred nobody completed, the missing piece being a failed init path.

questions.promptHtml: What does a "leaked coroutine" mean in Android, how do you detect one, and what tools do you reach for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Leaks are the most common long-term coroutine defect; this separates people who know the lifetime model from those who only know launch.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A leaked coroutine is one that outlives the thing it works for: a collector or request still running after its screen or owner is gone, or a job parked forever on something that never completes. Because a running coroutine is reachable from its dispatcher and its Job, everything it captures (Activity, view, big list) stays reachable too. I detect them with LeakCanary for the captured objects, counting children of long-lived scopes, a coroutine dump in JVM tests, and by auditing for scopes without an owner like GlobalScope or an uncancelled CoroutineScope(...)."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two shapes:

  1. Lifetime leak: coroutine runs after owner death. Sources: GlobalScope.launch, a hand-made CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main) in an Activity never cancelled, collecting SharedFlow (never completes) in a scope bigger than the UI, viewModelScope work holding a Context.
  2. Hang leak: suspended forever: CompletableDeferred never completed, Channel.receive with no sender and no close, Mutex never unlocked, suspendCancellableCoroutine where callback never fires and no invokeOnCancellation/timeout. The coroutine is cheap, but it pins its captured locals.

Why it retains memory: the continuation (state machine) holds spilled locals and this; the Job is referenced by the scope's Job children list and, if suspended on a callback, by the callback's owner.

Detection toolbox:

Symptom Tool
Activity/Fragment retained after destroy LeakCanary; heap path will show ...Continuation or DispatchedContinuation in chain
Growing thread/worker activity in background Perfetto / Android Studio CPU profiler thread view
Growing count in a scope scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count() logged in debug, or exposed via debug menu
Heap: many StandaloneCoroutine, SafeCollector, ChannelContinuation Android Studio heap dump, filter on kotlinx.coroutines
JVM test DebugProbes dump, runTest failing with uncompleted coroutines
Static Lint/detekt GlobalCoroutineUsage, InjectDispatcher, custom rule for CoroutineScope( outside DI

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Leaky: scope never cancelled, collects forever
class Tracker(ctx: Context) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main)        // owner? none
    init { scope.launch { locationFlow.collect { ctx.show(it) } } } // ctx captured
}

// Fixed: owner-bound
class Tracker(private val appScope: CoroutineScope) {
    fun start(owner: LifecycleOwner, ui: Ui) {
        owner.lifecycleScope.launch {
            owner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                locationFlow.collect { ui.show(it) }
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing "coroutines are lightweight so leaks don't matter"; the captured Activity is the heavy part.
  • Cancelling a scope's Job (scope.cancel()) then reusing the scope: it is dead, new launches silently do nothing.
  • Treating viewModelScope as safe for anything referencing a View/Context.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does LeakCanary see coroutine leaks? → Only the retained Activity/Fragment/ViewModel; the path to GC root shows the coroutine, which is the clue.
  2. Is a never-completing collect a leak? → Only if it outlives its owner; infinite collection inside a properly bound scope is normal.
  3. How do you bulk find unbounded scopes? → Grep/detekt for CoroutineScope(, GlobalScope; require injected scopes with defined owners.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use viewModelScope and cancel jobs." Senior: separates lifetime vs hang leaks, names retention path via continuation, brings tooling and static rules, and ties to API design (inject owner-bound scopes).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature kept an application-wide SharedFlow collector alive per opened screen; after a day of use, 300 live collectors each retained a destroyed Fragment's view hierarchy.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (800k DAU) shipped chat 7.2. Crashlytics shows OOM rate up from 0.15% to 0.9% of sessions on 3 GB RAM devices, mostly after 40+ minutes of use. Heap dump from QA shows 2,100 instances of ChatFragment$onViewCreated$1 continuations and 260 retained ChatFragment objects (user opened and left chats). Code:

class ChatRepo @Inject constructor(private val socket: Socket) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO)
    fun observe(chatId: String, onMsg: (Msg) -> Unit) {
        scope.launch { socket.messages(chatId).collect { onMsg(it) } }
    }
}
// in ChatFragment.onViewCreated:
repo.observe(chatId) { msg -> adapter.add(msg) }

The ChatRepo is @Singleton. The team suspects Glide image cache (red herring), and a recent RecyclerView upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix, and explain how you would prevent the class of bug.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase heap with largeHeap, clear Glide cache, upgrade LeakCanary." It treats the symptom and misses that the callback lambda captures the Fragment.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the leak scale with the number of chats opened? (yes means per-open leak). Is ChatFragment count in the heap equal to opens minus live? Did the Glide or RecyclerView version change? Any difference on Android 14 vs 9?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix release 7.2.1 making collection lifecycle-aware; roll out via staged rollout; remote flag to restrict to prior transport if available.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) per-open collector in a singleton scope capturing the Fragment; (b) adapter holding old views; (c) Glide request targets; (d) RecyclerView pool bug.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump in Android Studio: shortest path from GC root for a retained ChatFragment goes ChatRepo.scope -> JobSupport children -> StandaloneCoroutine -> ContinuationImpl -> lambda -> ChatFragment. Log scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count() in a debug overlay while opening/closing chats: grows by one per open. Disable Glide to see if memory still grows.
  5. Root cause: observe gives the Fragment's lambda a lifetime of the singleton's scope; collect on a socket flow never completes, so the coroutine, and the captured Fragment, live until process death.
  6. Fix: Short-term: return a Job and cancel in onDestroyView. Long-term: expose a Flow, collect from the lifecycle:
class ChatRepo @Inject constructor(private val socket: Socket) {
    fun messages(chatId: String): Flow<Msg> = socket.messages(chatId)
}
// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        repo.messages(chatId).collect { adapter.add(it) }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Ban callback-registering APIs that take lambdas plus an internal scope; LeakCanary in debug and in instrumented UI tests (LeakAssertions); a debug-only metric of live children on app scopes; code review rule "who owns this coroutine?".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No largeHeap; it delays the crash and slows GC. No WeakReference around the Fragment inside the lambda: it hides the leak and still keeps a running collector doing work.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• We need messages while the app is backgrounded for notifications. → That is a separate, explicitly app-scoped collector owned by a service/WorkManager, with a single instance, not one per screen.
  • Fix should keep one socket subscription across screens. → shareIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay = 0) at the repo, so screens add subscribers, not coroutines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "register listener + internal scope" convenience API shipped in a shared module and leaked in four different apps. The permanent fix was deleting the API, not teaching everyone to remember to cancel.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: memory flags and cache tweaks.
  • Hire: finds singleton scope capturing Fragment, cancels or uses lifecycle.
  • Strong hire: heap path evidence, shareIn trade-off, API redesign, prevention instrumentation, rejects weak-reference band-aids.

questions.promptHtml: How do you write a test that fails when code leaves a coroutine running? What does runTest give you for free and what does it not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Turns leak knowledge into prevention. Many candidates can describe leaks but have no automated safety net.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "runTest waits for its child coroutines and fails if they don't finish within the timeout, and it reports uncaught exceptions. Work launched in backgroundScope is cancelled at the end, so it never fails a test even if leaking, and anything launched in a scope outside the test is invisible to it. So for leak tests I inject the scope, run the action, cancel the owner, then assert on job.children or isActive, and for hangs I add DebugProbes with @CoroutinesTimeout."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
runTest (kotlinx-coroutines-test 1.7+ semantics) creates a TestScope with a StandardTestDispatcher, virtual time, and waits for the test body plus its children. Rules to remember:

  • Children of TestScope not completed: the test waits; if still pending after the timeout (default 60 s wall time in recent versions, configurable via timeout parameter; verify in your version), it fails with a message listing active coroutines.
  • backgroundScope.launch is for infinite collectors; cancelled automatically at the end, so you get no failure.
  • this.coroutineContext.job.children can be asserted.
  • A scope you construct yourself with real Dispatchers is not controlled by runTest. Inject CoroutineScope(coroutineContext) or a TestScope instead.

Pattern for owner-lifecycle tests:

create owner with injected scope S (child of TestScope)
owner.start()                -> children(S) == 1
owner.stop()/onCleared()     -> advanceUntilIdle(); children(S) == 0

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Poller(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val api: Api) {
    private var job: Job? = null
    fun start() { job = scope.launch { while (isActive) { api.poll(); delay(1_000) } } }
    fun stop() { job?.cancel() }
}

@Test fun `stop cancels polling`() = runTest {
    val scopeJob = Job(coroutineContext.job)
    val poller = Poller(CoroutineScope(coroutineContext + scopeJob), FakeApi())
    poller.start()
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals(1, scopeJob.children.count())
    poller.stop()
    runCurrent()
    assertEquals(0, scopeJob.children.count())   // would fail if stop() forgot to cancel
    scopeJob.cancel()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using backgroundScope for the thing under test and thinking green means no leak.
  • Real dispatcher in the class under test, so the test passes before the coroutine even runs.
  • Forgetting Dispatchers.setMain for viewModelScope classes (use MainDispatcherRule).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you test viewModelScope is cancelled? → Call onCleared indirectly via ViewModelStore.clear() and assert collector stopped via a fake's subscriber count.
  2. What if the leak is a never-resumed suspendCancellableCoroutine? → Test that cancelling the caller triggers invokeOnCancellation unregistration on the fake.
  3. Can this run in instrumented tests? → Use LeakCanary's DetectLeaksAfterTestSuccess rule in UI tests.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use runTest and advanceUntilIdle." Senior: knows what runTest does and does not catch, designs classes for injectable scopes, asserts on Job structure, and adds LeakCanary in instrumentation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A polling class passed all unit tests for a year because tests used backgroundScope; a children-count assertion later caught a missing cancel after a refactor.

questions.promptHtml: How expensive is a coroutine in memory and CPU compared with a thread, and where does the real overhead show up in an Android app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors must justify "coroutines are cheap" with mechanism, and know where the claim breaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A coroutine is a heap object graph, not an OS thread: a Job plus a compiler-generated state-machine continuation holding the live locals, on the order of low hundreds of bytes, so 100k of them is tens of MB at most, whereas 100k threads is impossible. Switching between them is a dispatch of a Runnable, not a kernel context switch. The real costs are allocation and GC from short-lived suspend calls, dispatcher hops, and over-parallelising work on a small thread pool."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Creation of launch: allocates a StandaloneCoroutine (a JobSupport with state, list of children/handlers), a DispatchedContinuation on dispatch, and the user lambda's SuspendLambda state machine. Each suspend call that actually suspends may allocate a continuation object for that function (only when it suspends: the compiler reuses the continuation per invocation via the label trick; allocated at first call of the function). A suspend function that never suspends at runtime still allocates its continuation object on entry in most cases, which is why tiny hot suspend functions (called in tight loops) can show GC pressure; the compiler skips it for tail-call suspend functions that only call another suspend in tail position.

Numbers (state as estimates, measure yourself): thread = about 1 MB reserved virtual stack on ART (physical commit much smaller) plus kernel structures; creating one costs on the order of tens to 100+ microseconds. Coroutine = on the order of 100-500 bytes plus captured variables; launching 100k on Default typically completes in tens of ms. Math: 100,000 × ~300 B = 30 MB worst, versus threads 100,000 × 1 MB = 100 GB virtual, which the OS will refuse.

Where it still hurts:

  1. Dispatcher hops: withContext(IO) inside a loop of 10k iterations creates 10k context switches plus allocation; batch the loop inside one withContext.
  2. Flow operator chains: each operator wraps a FlowCollector lambda; a flowOn adds a channel (buffer 64 by default) and a coroutine.
  3. Channel/Flow per item: flow { emit } for 1 element across a hot path.
  4. Thread pool saturation: Default has core-count threads; CPU work beyond that queues. IO (max(64, cores)) sharing the same pool, with blocking calls, starves other work.
  5. Debug mode / DebugProbes adds cost; don't benchmark with it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Slow: 10k hops, each allocates and re-dispatches
items.forEach { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.insert(it) } }

// Fast: one hop, one transaction
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { dao.insertAll(items) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Parallelising 3 ms tasks with async where scheduling overhead exceeds the work.
  • Measuring in a debug build with the debugger attached.
  • Believing Dispatchers.IO makes blocking free: it just has more threads (64 or cores).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a context switch between coroutines free? → No: cheap, but it is a dispatch (queue push, wake a worker if needed) and cache effects.
  2. How do you measure? → Macrobenchmark / Microbenchmark with allocation counts, Perfetto traces, Debug.startAllocCounting style tools on the profiler.
  3. What bounds IO parallelism? → Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) creates a view that caps concurrency without new threads.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Coroutines are lightweight threads." Senior: says what is allocated, gives rough numbers with math, names the real overheads (hops, allocation in hot loops, pool saturation), and admits to measuring instead of assuming.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A sync loop with withContext per row took 9 s for 20k rows; moving the hop outside the loop and batching inserts brought it to 600 ms.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo app uploads 50,000 queued images in a background sync on app start after a long offline period. Current code:

suspend fun syncAll(items: List<Photo>) = coroutineScope {
    items.map { async(Dispatchers.IO) { upload(it) } }.awaitAll()
}

On mid-range devices (4 GB RAM, 8 cores) Perfetto shows UI jank (p95 frame time 38 ms), OkHttp reporting SocketTimeoutExceptions at 22 percent, the process sits at 480 MB, and battery-drain complaints are rising. upload does a 2 MB file read, compress, and OkHttp call. The backend rate-limits at 10 concurrent requests per user.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you restructure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Coroutines are cheap, so 50k is fine; just increase timeouts." Ignores that cheap coroutines still start 50k simultaneous bitmaps and sockets.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does it need to finish while foreground? (WorkManager vs foreground). Server concurrency limit per user (10)? Is order important? Partial failure policy? Memory cost per upload (2 MB buffer × concurrency)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap concurrency to 4 right now with a semaphore; defer start by 10 s after launch to protect startup.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded concurrency (50k tasks × 2 MB buffers) causing memory and GC jank; (b) OkHttp dispatcher caps (64 total, 5 per host) queueing calls so timeouts start counting in queue; (c) server throttling; (d) red herring: coroutine count itself.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android Studio memory profiler for allocation spikes; Perfetto for GC and thread states; OkHttp EventListener for queue time vs network time; server 429 counts.
  5. Root cause: All 50k async blocks start immediately and each allocates its buffer after hitting an IO thread, so working set grows with queue length; calls wait in OkHttp's queue past the read timeout window.
  6. Fix: Bound concurrency, keep memory per item bounded, make it resumable:
suspend fun syncAll(items: List<Photo>) = coroutineScope {
    val limit = Semaphore(4)
    items.map { p ->
        async(Dispatchers.IO) { limit.withPermit { upload(p) } }
    }.awaitAll()
}
// 50k pending asyncs are still 50k small objects; better:
suspend fun syncAll2(items: List<Photo>) {
    items.asFlow().flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { p -> flow { emit(upload(p)) } }.collect()
}

Or channelFlow with 4 workers. Move it to WorkManager with constraints (unmetered/charging), chunked batches of 200 with progress persisted. 7. Prevention: Load test with 50k fixture; allocation budget in a benchmark; code review rule "every fan-out has an explicit concurrency bound". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not increasing OkHttp dispatcher limits (backend rate limit is 10). Not Dispatchers.IO with 64 threads as the throttle: that is an accident, not a design. limitedParallelism(4) is acceptable but semaphore/flatMapMerge states intent.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• One upload fails; should others continue? → In coroutineScope one failure cancels all; use supervisorScope/per-item runCatching (rethrowing cancellation) and a retry queue.
  • 8 workers is faster on Wi-Fi. → Adaptive concurrency: start at 4, raise on low latency; cap by server limit.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite from a sync engine: replacing unbounded awaitAll with bounded flatMapMerge(4) cut peak memory from 480 MB to 90 MB and, counter-intuitively, total time fell because timeouts and retries disappeared.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases timeouts or blames coroutines.
  • Hire: bounds concurrency, identifies memory and rate limit.
  • Strong hire: quantifies memory, notes OkHttp queueing, WorkManager, failure semantics, adaptive concurrency.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a coroutine and a thread? Isn't a coroutine just a lightweight thread?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline check; "lightweight thread" is the lazy answer, and seniors should correct it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A thread is an OS-scheduled unit with its own stack that blocks when it waits. A coroutine is a suspendable computation managed by a library: when it waits it suspends, saving its state in a heap object and freeing the thread to run something else. It is not a lightweight thread; it runs on threads chosen by a dispatcher, can hop between them, and is cancelled cooperatively with structured parent-child lifetimes."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Key differences:

Aspect Thread Coroutine
Scheduling Preemptive by OS Cooperative: switches only at suspension points
Waiting Blocks the thread Suspends; thread is released
State storage Native stack (about 1 MB reserved) Heap continuation, spilled locals
Cost Heavy to create, limited count Cheap, 100k+ feasible
Cancellation interrupt() plus manual flag, unreliable Cooperative, propagates down the Job tree
Failure Uncaught handler per thread Propagates up the Job tree (supervisor excepted)
Lifetime Free-floating Structured: parent waits for children

Mechanism: the Kotlin compiler performs CPS transformation. suspend fun gets an extra Continuation parameter; the body becomes a state machine with a label. At a suspension point the function returns the sentinel COROUTINE_SUSPENDED; the thread unwinds. Later, the continuation's resumeWith is called by whoever completes the awaited thing (via the dispatcher), re-entering at the saved label. Because there is no preemption, a CPU-bound loop without suspension points or ensureActive() blocks its thread and cannot be cancelled.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// blocks a thread for 1s
Thread.sleep(1_000)
// suspends; thread is free for others
delay(1_000)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling blocking APIs (Thread.sleep, JDBC, InputStream.read) in a coroutine and expecting suspension.
  • Assuming a coroutine is pinned to a thread; thread-locals break across suspension.
  • Assuming coroutines are parallel by themselves; they are concurrent, and parallel only with a multi-thread dispatcher.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does launch create a thread? → No; it schedules on a dispatcher's existing threads.
  2. Can a single thread run many coroutines? → Yes, e.g. Main.
  3. What is the "colored function" cost? → suspend is part of the signature and viral; bridging to blocking code needs runBlocking (avoid on Main) or withContext.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Lighter than threads." Senior: cooperative vs preemptive, CPS state machine, release-the-thread semantics, structured concurrency, and the blocking-call trap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "coroutine-ised" legacy module still called blocking socket reads inside Dispatchers.Default, saturating the 8-thread pool and freezing unrelated features.

questions.promptHtml: How do coroutines compare with ExecutorService/AsyncTask/HandlerThread, and how do you bridge an existing Executor into coroutines?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many Android codebases still contain Executors; seniors must reason about coexistence and know what coroutines add.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Executors give you a thread pool and a Future, but no structured lifetime, no composition without callbacks, and cancellation via interrupt that blocking code may ignore. AsyncTask is deprecated since API 30 and had Activity-leak and serial-execution problems. Coroutines add structured scopes, cooperative cancellation, and sequential-looking code. I bridge with executor.asCoroutineDispatcher() and own its shutdown."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Executor: you submit Runnables. Results come as Future.get() (blocks) or callbacks. Cancellation: future.cancel(true) interrupts the thread, which only works if the code checks interrupts or does interruptible I/O. No parent-child.
  • AsyncTask (deprecated API 30): doInBackground ran on a shared serial executor since Android 3.0, results delivered on Main; inner-class leaks; no cancel guarantee.
  • HandlerThread/Looper: single-thread message loop, good for ordered work; coroutines can model it as a single-thread dispatcher or handler.asCoroutineDispatcher().

Bridge: val d = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4).asCoroutineDispatcher() gives an ExecutorCoroutineDispatcher. It is Closeable: you must close() it, or the threads leak (the non-daemon default thread factory keeps the process alive on JVM). For a long-lived app, prefer Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) which shares IO's threads and needs no shutdown. Reserve a custom executor dispatcher for libraries (OkHttp's dispatcher executor, Room's query executor) that already own threads.

Bridging in the other direction: Executor API taking callback; wrap with suspendCancellableCoroutine, or ListenableFuture.await() (kotlinx-coroutines-guava).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Reuse an existing library executor
val dbDispatcher = roomExecutor.asCoroutineDispatcher()

// Preferred when you just need a bound
private val parser = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(2)

// Future -> suspend (guava / androidx concurrent-futures)
suspend fun fetch(): Data = api.fetchFuture().await()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating newFixedThreadPool dispatchers per call and never closing them.
  • Assuming future.cancel(true) stops a coroutine-wrapped blocking call; it does not unless it is interruptible.
  • Wrapping blocking Future.get() in a coroutine on Default.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Executor vs limitedParallelism? → The latter shares threads, no shutdown; semantics are concurrency cap, not thread identity.
  2. Does a single-thread executor give mutual exclusion? → Yes for code that does not suspend; across suspension points state can interleave, so prefer Mutex or confinement with care.
  3. What replaced AsyncTask in your codebase? → ViewModel + coroutines, WorkManager for deferrable work.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Coroutines are simpler than AsyncTask." Senior: compares cancellation and lifetime semantics, knows the dispatcher bridge and its closing duty, and prefers limitedParallelism.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library migration leaked 8 non-daemon threads per screen because an asCoroutineDispatcher() was created in a ViewModel and never closed.

questions.promptHtml: What problems do coroutines solve compared with callbacks, and how do you correctly wrap a callback API as a suspend function or a Flow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Callback wrapping is a daily task, and the correct version (cancellation, single resume) is a classic bug source.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Callbacks give inversion of control: no return value, nesting, manual error plumbing, and no cancellation story. Coroutines restore sequential code, normal try/catch, and structured cancellation. To wrap a one-shot callback I use suspendCancellableCoroutine, resume exactly once, and unregister in invokeOnCancellation. For many-shot callbacks I use callbackFlow with trySend and awaitClose { unregister }."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Problems with callbacks: nested "pyramid", error handling split between onError and thrown exceptions, hard to cancel, lifecycle leaks (callback holds Activity), hard to compose parallel and sequential steps, thread of callback unspecified.

Wrapping rules:

  1. One-shot: suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont -> }. Must call resume/resumeWithException at most once (a second call throws IllegalStateException: Already resumed). Register cont.invokeOnCancellation { call.cancel() }.
  2. Multi-shot: callbackFlow { }. Must end with awaitClose { }, else it throws IllegalStateException("'awaitClose { yourCallbackOrListener.cancel() }' should be used in the end of callbackFlow block"). Use trySend in non-suspending callbacks; buffer defaults to 64 (BUFFERED), set .conflate() for latest-only.
  3. Threading: the callback thread is whatever the API uses; resume dispatches back through the continuation's dispatcher, so no manual runOnUiThread.
  4. suspendCoroutine (non-cancellable) loses cancellation: the caller is cancelled but the call keeps running and the resume is ignored.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
suspend fun Call.await(): Response = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    enqueue(object : Callback {
        override fun onResponse(call: Call, response: Response) = cont.resume(response)
        override fun onFailure(call: Call, e: IOException) {
            if (!cont.isCancelled) cont.resumeWithException(e)
        }
    })
    cont.invokeOnCancellation { cancel() }
}

fun LocationClient.updates(): Flow<Location> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = object : LocationCallback() {
        override fun onLocationResult(r: LocationResult) { trySend(r.lastLocation!!) }
    }
    requestUpdates(cb)
    awaitClose { removeUpdates(cb) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using suspendCoroutine for cancellable work.
  • Resuming twice (success and a later error callback).
  • Using send (suspending) from a non-suspend callback, or forgetting the callback unregistration so the producer leaks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the callback fires after cancellation? → resume on a cancelled continuation is ignored (safe); use tryResume patterns only when needed.
  2. Backpressure in callbackFlow? → Bounded channel; choose conflate or buffer; trySend returns a failed result when full with SUSPEND... in practice use buffer or drop strategy explicitly.
  3. When use CompletableDeferred? → Bridging a single result with external completion, not for cancel-aware registration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Use suspendCoroutine to wrap." Senior: insists on cancellable variant, unregisters in cancellation, handles double-resume, picks callbackFlow buffer semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A Bluetooth wrapper used suspendCoroutine; screens closed mid-scan kept the scanner running and drained battery until scan timeout.

questions.promptHtml: Compare Kotlin coroutines/Flow with RxJava on semantics, not just syntax. What differs in threading, error handling, cancellation, backpressure, and hot/cold behavior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior candidates at product companies often inherit Rx codebases; they must reason about the real differences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Rx is a push-based library with many types (Observable, Flowable, Single, Completable, Maybe), explicit Schedulers, Disposables and an onError terminal channel. Coroutines are a language feature plus library: one suspend for single values, Flow for streams, dispatchers via context, structured concurrency instead of CompositeDisposable, and cancellation is cooperative through exceptions. Backpressure in Flow is built in by suspension; Rx needs Flowable."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dimension RxJava 2/3 Coroutines / Flow
Single value Single/Maybe/Completable suspend fun (nullable or Unit)
Stream Observable/Flowable Flow<T>
Backpressure Flowable only (reactive-streams request(n)); Observable has none Producer suspends; plus buffer/conflate
Threading subscribeOn (where it subscribes), observeOn (downstream hops) flowOn (upstream only), withContext; collector context preserved
Lifetime Disposable, CompositeDisposable, AutoDispose/lifecycle libs Job hierarchy, viewModelScope, repeatOnLifecycle
Errors onError terminal; operators onErrorReturn, retry exceptions; catch (upstream only), retry, try/catch around collect
Hot sources Subjects, publish().refCount() SharedFlow, StateFlow, shareIn, stateIn
Null Rx2+ forbids null in streams Allowed
Debugging Assembly stack traces need RxJavaPlugins.setOnObservableAssembly tricks Debug mode, stack-trace recovery, IDE debugger
Testing TestScheduler, TestObserver runTest, virtual time, Turbine (third-party)
Operator breadth Very large (window, groupBy, buffer variants, timed ops) Smaller; extensible via transform / channelFlow
Platform Java, works anywhere Kotlin; multiplatform

Semantic differences that bite:

  • Cancellation: Rx dispose() stops delivery and unsubscribes; running blocking code inside is not interrupted unless the source honours it (it may interrupt a Schedulers.io() thread). Coroutines cancel at suspension points, and cancellation propagates to children.
  • Errors after dispose: Rx emits UndeliverableException to the global handler (RxJavaPlugins.onError), and on Android with no handler it crashes. Coroutines route to the parent scope or CoroutineExceptionHandler.
  • Exceptions are not special in Flow: a failure in a collector throws through collect; Rx splits them between onNext and onError.
  • Laziness: both cold by default.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Rx
api.user(id).subscribeOn(io).observeOn(main)
    .subscribe({ ui.show(it) }, { ui.error(it) })
    .addTo(disposables)

// Coroutines
viewModelScope.launch {
    try { ui.show(api.user(id)) } catch (e: IOException) { ui.error(e) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating observeOn with flowOn; flowOn only affects upstream.
  • Assuming coroutines remove the need for backpressure thinking; unbounded buffer still leaks memory.
  • Treating Rx's global error handler as optional.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Flow a drop-in for Flowable? → Close for semantics (suspension), but no request(n) fine control; conformance to reactive streams needs asPublisher.
  2. Which is faster? → Depends; Flow has fewer allocations for simple chains, Rx has mature optimised operator fusion; measure for hot paths.
  3. Why does Rx testing feel easier to some? → Synchronous TestScheduler; but runTest gives equivalent virtual time.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Coroutines are simpler, Rx is older." Senior: contrasts schedulers vs context, Disposable vs Job, error channel semantics, UndeliverableException, backpressure, and testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During a migration, RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler was missing in a new module; a late network error after dispose crashed 0.4% of sessions with UndeliverableException.

questions.promptHtml: Your team lead says "kill Rx, move everything to coroutines." When would you argue that RxJava should stay?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests judgment and avoiding dogma; seniors weigh cost, risk, and capabilities.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I'd migrate new code and touch-points, but keep Rx where the cost-benefit is negative: large stable Rx-heavy modules that rarely change, features using Rx's richer time-window operators, code shared with Java-only modules or libraries exposing Rx types, and teams with strong Rx expertise on a tight delivery schedule. A big-bang rewrite adds regression risk without user value, so I'd make Rx boundaries explicit and migrate by use."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Legit reasons to keep Rx:

  1. Operator richness: window, buffer(timespan, count), groupBy, publish(selector), replay with time bounds, throttleFirst, sample variants, join. Flow can express most with channelFlow/transform, but hand-written equivalents carry bug risk.
  2. Third-party Rx APIs: RxBinding, RxPermissions, RxBle, RxRelay, older SDKs. Interop via kotlinx-coroutines-rx2/rx3 is fine for edges.
  3. Java modules: Java code cannot call suspend ergonomically; Rx or CompletableFuture is friendlier.
  4. Testing: existing TestScheduler suites that cover tricky timing; rewriting tests costs more than rewriting code.
  5. Reactive Streams compliance: backpressure protocols with other systems.
  6. Risk and cost: a 150k-line Rx layer that is stable has near-zero defects per quarter; rewriting trades known behavior for unknown. Estimate: if 40 engineer-weeks to migrate and the module changes twice a year, payoff is poor.

Reasons not to keep Rx: RxJava 2 is end-of-life (Feb 2021), RxJava 3 is in maintenance mode, lifecycle handling needs extra libraries, Kotlin Multiplatform is impossible, new hires increasingly know coroutines, and mixing doubles cognitive load and test infrastructure. So the real rule: no new Rx code, migrate on touch, keep a facade at module boundaries.

Decision matrix:

Situation Choice
New feature Coroutines/Flow
Rx module, high churn Migrate incrementally
Rx module, stable, low churn Leave, wrap at boundary
Java library API Keep Rx/Future facade
Complex time-window pipeline Keep Rx or port carefully with tests

interface Orders { suspend fun get(id: String): Order; fun updates(): Flow<Order> }

class RxOrders(private val legacy: LegacyOrderService) : Orders {

questions.subtopic: Rx operator to Flow operator mapping
questions.promptHtml: Map the common RxJava operators and types to their coroutine/Flow equivalents. Which ones have no direct equivalent or behave differently?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The practical core of any migration; mistakes here become subtle behavior regressions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Single/Maybe/Completable become suspend functions; Observable/Flowable become Flow; Subjects become SharedFlow/StateFlow; Disposable becomes Job. switchMap is flatMapLatest, flatMap is flatMapMerge, concatMap is flatMapConcat, combineLatest is combine, observeOn/subscribeOn collapse into flowOn, which only moves upstream. throttleFirst, buffer(count)/window need custom code, and retry, onErrorReturn map to retry and catch { emit }."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
RxJava Kotlin Notes
Single<T> suspend fun(): T Errors are exceptions
Maybe<T> suspend fun(): T?
Completable suspend fun()
Observable/Flowable Flow<T>
map, filter, take, skip(drop), scan map, filter, take, drop, scan/runningFold
flatMap flatMapMerge(concurrency) Default concurrency 16 (DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY); Rx unlimited
concatMap flatMapConcat
switchMap flatMapLatest
combineLatest combine
zip zip
merge merge
startWith onStart { emit(x) }
doOnNext / doOnSubscribe / doOnComplete onEach / onStart / onCompletion
onErrorReturn catch { emit(x) } catch is upstream only
retry(n) / retryWhen retry(n) / retryWhen
debounce debounce
throttleLatest sample (not identical)
throttleFirst none; custom transform
distinctUntilChanged distinctUntilChanged
timeout timeout (Flow, @FlowPreview in some versions) or withTimeout
observeOn(x) flowOn upstream only; collector uses its own context No downstream shift
subscribeOn(x) flowOn(x)
PublishSubject MutableSharedFlow(replay=0)
BehaviorSubject MutableStateFlow StateFlow conflates and requires an initial value
ReplaySubject(n) MutableSharedFlow(replay=n)
share()/publish().refCount() shareIn(scope, WhileSubscribed())
replay(1).autoConnect() shareIn(scope, Lazily, replay=1)
Disposable/CompositeDisposable Job/CoroutineScope
blockingGet runBlocking avoid on Main
window, buffer(count), groupBy custom (channelFlow, chunked helpers) confirm availability in your version

Behavior differences to flag: StateFlow equality-conflates (Rx BehaviorSubject emits repeats), flatMapMerge defaults to concurrency 16 whereas Rx flatMap is unbounded, combine waits for all sources, and catch does not catch downstream exceptions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Rx: search-as-you-type
query.debounce(300, MILLISECONDS).distinctUntilChanged()
     .switchMap { api.search(it).toObservable() }.observeOn(main)

// Flow
queryFlow.debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged()
    .flatMapLatest { flow { emit(api.search(it)) } }
    .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)   // affects upstream of this point only

• Using flowOn expecting observeOn behavior.

questions.contextHtml: A fintech Android app (4M MAU, 380k LOC, 14 modules) is built on RxJava 2 with MVP. RxJava 2 has been end-of-life since 2021. The team of 18 wants coroutines. Leadership asks for a plan; roadmap has two feature-critical quarters ahead. Crash-free rate is 99.7%, and a payments module (35k LOC, heavy combineLatest, retryWhen, window-based rate limiting) changes about twice a year. A proposal exists to freeze features for one quarter and rewrite everything.
questions.promptHtml: Do you approve the rewrite? What do you propose instead, and how do you decide per module?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, rewrite everything to Flow; it is cleaner." Ignores risk, opportunity cost, and measurable payoff. Or "no, never touch it" without a path.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the actual pain (hiring, bugs, Rx2 EOL security, KMP plans)? Churn per module over the last year? Test coverage per module? Which modules block Compose/Android upgrades? Is there a business deadline?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed, no incident; instead stop the bleeding of new Rx: policy "no new Rx" and lint rule enforcing it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most pain is in high-churn UI/presentation modules; (b) payments core is stable and risky to port; (c) hiring/onboarding friction is the real driver; (d) EOL concerns mostly around RxJava 2 → upgrade path to 3 is cheap and separate.
  4. How I'd verify each: Git churn analysis per module, defect density from Jira, test coverage reports, survey onboarding time, check Rx dependency count in modules.
  5. Root cause: The question is investment allocation, not technology: migrating costs engineer-weeks with delayed payoff.
  6. Fix (plan): Reject the big-bang rewrite. Plan: (1) Upgrade Rx2 → Rx3 mechanically (RxJava3 has a migration tool/rename; keep kotlinx-coroutines-rx3) in one low-risk PR series. (2) Add repository facades exposing suspend/Flow, internals still Rx. (3) New features and touched presentation code in ViewModel + coroutines. (4) Migrate by churn: top 3 high-churn modules first; characterization tests before each. (5) Payments core last, with ported window logic only if business value; otherwise keep Rx behind a facade permanently. (6) Track: % of public APIs suspend/Flow, Rx dependency count, crash rate.
  7. Prevention: Lint banning io.reactivex imports in new modules, architecture tests (ArchUnit-like) for layer boundaries, dashboards for migration progress.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a feature freeze (6-quarter roadmap risk); not rewrite payments core under deadline; not mixing Rx and Flow inside a single pipeline.

questions.contextHtml: You are migrating the order-tracking feature of a food-delivery app (2.5M DAU, peak 18k orders/min) from RxJava 3 to coroutines while it serves live traffic. The feature has OrderRepository (Rx, 22 call sites across 9 ViewModels), a websocket Observable<OrderEvent> shared via publish().refCount(), and a BehaviorSubject<Order> cache. Rules: no big-bang, each release must be shippable, rollback must be possible per release, crash-free must stay at or above 99.8%. The team has kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 available.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out the migration sequence, the interop seams, and how you protect production at each step.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Convert repository to Flow and fix compile errors in all 9 ViewModels." That is a big-bang change with no seams, no flags, and no tests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which streams are hot (websocket) and who shares them? Where are the thread assumptions (main-safe callers)? Is there test coverage of event ordering? Can we flag by user cohort? What is the latency budget for order updates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident, so the "mitigation" is safety nets first: characterization tests of current ordering/retry behavior, a remote flag per migrated repo method, and a global RxJava error handler to ensure no UndeliverableException crashes while mixing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (where it will go wrong): (a) hot/cold and sharing differences (refCount vs shareIn), (b) cancellation difference leaving websocket subscriptions open, (c) threading (observeOn(main) assumptions), (d) conflation difference (BehaviorSubject vs StateFlow).
  4. How I'd verify each: Record production event sequences (fixtures) and replay through both implementations in a differential test; count live websocket subscriptions via metrics; LeakCanary and Job.children counts in debug; shadow-read mode comparing outputs in a staging cohort.
  5. Root cause (the plan's logic): Make the seam the repository interface, not the internals. Migrate leaf-to-root: data source, then repository, then ViewModel; interop adapters keep both sides valid.
  6. Fix (sequence):
    • Step 1: Define OrderRepository with suspend fun get(id) and fun events(id): Flow<OrderEvent>; implement it over the existing Rx via adapters (single.await(), observable.asFlow()).
    • Step 2: Move ViewModels one by one to the new interface; each PR small, flagged.
    • Step 3: Replace the implementation internals: websocket becomes callbackFlow, shared with shareIn(appScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay = 1); cache StateFlow.
    • Step 4: Remove adapters and the Rx dependency when call sites hit zero.
class OrderRepoAdapter(private val rx: RxOrderRepository) : OrderRepository {
    override suspend fun get(id: String): Order = rx.order(id).await()
    override fun events(id: String): Flow<OrderEvent> = rx.events(id).asFlow()
}
  1. Prevention: Differential tests, kill switch per method, dashboards of subscriptions and error rates; lint rule banning Rx in migrated packages.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not converting ViewModel and repository in the same PR. Not exposing Flow to Java callers without a bridge. Not keeping BehaviorSubject semantics via SharedFlow(replay=1) by default.

  • Event ordering regressed in canary. → Check flatMapMerge vs concatMap choice; ordering requires flatMapConcat.

  • Strong hire: differential/shadow testing, flags, hot-stream sharing semantics, cancellation and subscription metrics, rollback plan.

questions.promptHtml: How do you interoperate between RxJava 3 and coroutines using kotlinx-coroutines-rx3, and what happens to cancellation and disposal across the bridge?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Real migrations live on these bridges for months; mistakes cause leaks and lost errors.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "kotlinx-coroutines-rx3 gives await(), awaitSingle(), awaitFirst() for Single/Maybe/Completable/Observable, asFlow() for Observable/Flowable, and Flow.asObservable()/asFlowable() plus builders rxSingle, rxObservable, rxFlowable, rxCompletable. Cancelling the coroutine disposes the Rx subscription, and disposing the Rx stream cancels the coroutine. The catches are error routing after disposal and thread/dispatcher differences."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Directions:

  1. Rx to coroutines: single.await() subscribes, suspends, and on cancellation of the awaiting coroutine disposes the upstream. observable.asFlow() collects with backpressure bridging (it subscribes with a buffer; upstream Observable has no backpressure, so a slow collector buffers, potentially unbounded, so add .conflate()/buffer consciously).
  2. Coroutines to Rx: rxSingle(Dispatchers.IO) { api.get() } runs the block per subscription; dispose() cancels the coroutine. flow.asObservable() collects when subscribed. These preserve laziness.
  3. Scheduler/dispatcher: Scheduler.asCoroutineDispatcher() lets you run coroutines on an Rx scheduler (useful with a test scheduler); there is also a reverse adapter to make a Scheduler from a dispatcher (check the exact name in your version).
  4. Errors: Rx onError(e) becomes the thrown exception from await(). Coroutines to Rx: exception in rxSingle block goes to onError, but if the subscriber was disposed first, the exception goes to RxJavaPlugins.onError (undeliverable); install an error handler at app start.
  5. Null: awaitFirstOrNull etc. for empty streams; await() on empty Maybe throws NoSuchElementException unless using awaitSingleOrNull.

Cancellation diagram:

viewModelScope.launch { single.await() }
   scope cancelled --> await() cancellation --> Disposable.dispose() --> upstream stops
rxSingle { suspend work }.subscribe()
   disposable.dispose() --> coroutine job.cancel() --> CancellationException inside block

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// RxJava3 -> coroutines
suspend fun profile(): Profile = legacyApi.profile(id).awaitSingle()
fun ticks(): Flow<Tick> = legacyApi.ticks().asFlow().conflate()

// coroutines -> RxJava3 (for a not-yet-migrated caller)
fun profileRx(): Single<Profile> = rxSingle(Dispatchers.IO) { newRepo.profile(id) }

// App start
RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler { e ->
    if (e is UndeliverableException) Log.w("Rx", "undeliverable", e.cause) else throw e
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Catching Throwable around await() and swallowing CancellationException.
  • Using asFlow() on a fast Observable without a buffer decision.
  • Forgetting that rxSingle runs per subscription: two subscribers = two executions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which artifact for RxJava 2? → kotlinx-coroutines-rx2; reactive-streams Publisher has kotlinx-coroutines-reactive.
  2. How to test bridged code? → Use Schedulers.trampoline or RxJavaPlugins.setIoSchedulerHandler plus runTest; or convert the test scheduler with asCoroutineDispatcher().
  3. Does observeOn still apply after asFlow()? → The Flow collects in the collector's context; Rx scheduler hops before asFlow() still happen upstream.

sections.html: 3-YOE: lists await and asFlow. Senior: describes cancellation both ways, undeliverable errors, per-subscription execution of rx* builders, buffering on asFlow, and null/empty handling.
