questions.promptHtml: Why can an RxJava app crash with UndeliverableException while a coroutines app with the same bug usually does not? Compare how errors travel in each model.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Error propagation is where migrations produce production crashes; this probes real understanding of both models.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "In Rx, an error is a terminal signal delivered to onError. If the stream is already disposed or terminated, there is nobody to deliver it to, so RxJava 2/3 routes it to RxJavaPlugins.onError, which by default calls the thread's uncaught handler and crashes Android. In coroutines, an exception propagates up the Job hierarchy to the parent; if it reaches a root with no handler it goes to the thread's uncaught handler, but a cancelled coroutine's exceptions are mostly dropped or attached as suppressed, so late errors after cancellation don't crash."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rx rules: onError and onComplete are mutually exclusive terminal events; after disposal, emissions are ignored but an error from the source (e.g. IOException from a socket closed by the dispose) has no observer, thus "undeliverable". Rx 1 swallowed these; Rx 2 chose not to. UndeliverableException wraps it; if the cause is IOException or InterruptedException it is usually benign (network cancelled), and the recommended handler ignores those and rethrows programming errors (NullPointerException, IllegalStateException, etc.).

Coroutine rules:

  • Exception in launch child cancels parent (unless Supervisor), siblings cancelled, parent rethrows to its parent, up to the root. Root launch: goes to CoroutineExceptionHandler or thread uncaught handler. Root async: stored until await.
  • If a coroutine is already cancelled, a further exception becomes suppressed on the primary one or is dropped (non-cancellation exceptions after cancellation are reported to the handler only in specific cases such as thrown from invokeOnCompletion; typical late failures of cancelled suspendCancellableCoroutine resumes are ignored).
  • CancellationException is ignored for crash purposes.
  • Flow: exceptions propagate through collect; catch handles upstream only.

Comparison:

Event Rx Coroutines
Error before dispose/cancel onError thrown to awaiter or parent
Error after dispose/cancel Undeliverable, global handler, crash by default Dropped or suppressed
Silent swallowing risk Missing onError in subscribe = OnErrorNotImplementedException crash Unawaited async hides error until await/scope failure
Cancellation as error dispose is silent CancellationException must be rethrown
Central hook RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler CoroutineExceptionHandler (root coroutines only)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
RxJavaPlugins.setErrorHandler { e ->
    val cause = if (e is UndeliverableException) e.cause else e
    when (cause) {
        is IOException, is InterruptedException -> Unit // benign: disposed during I/O
        else -> Thread.currentThread().uncaughtExceptionHandler
            ?.uncaughtException(Thread.currentThread(), cause ?: e)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Subscribing with only onNext (Rx) and getting OnErrorNotImplementedException.
  • Assuming CoroutineExceptionHandler catches errors of children launched within coroutineScope.
  • Swallowing all exceptions in the Rx handler, hiding real bugs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does CoroutineExceptionHandler apply? → Only installed at root coroutines (or in the scope context) for launch; not for async results.
  2. How do you surface a stream error to UI without crashing? → Convert to state: catch { emit(UiState.Error) } in Flow; onErrorReturn/Result in Rx.
  3. What replaces onErrorResumeNext? → catch { emitAll(fallback) }.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Add an Rx global handler." Senior: explains why undeliverable exists, which causes are benign, how coroutine cancellation avoids it, and the handler's scope limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A crash cluster of UndeliverableException(IOException) appeared right after users backgrounded the app mid-request; a three-line global handler removed 0.3% of crashes.

questions.contextHtml:
After porting a ViewModel from Rx to Flow, QA reports: (1) the search results sometimes show the previous query's results; (2) the loading spinner never resets when the user retries the same query; (3) after a network error the screen stops reacting to any further queries; (4) UI updates sometimes happen off the main thread, crash rate 0.2% with CalledFromWrongThreadException. Original Rx used switchMap, BehaviorSubject, onErrorReturn, observeOn(main). Ported code:

class SearchVM(private val api: Api) : ViewModel() {
    private val query = MutableStateFlow("")
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UiState>(UiState.Idle)
    val state: StateFlow<UiState> = _state

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            query
                .debounce(300)
                .flatMapMerge { q -> flow { emit(api.search(q)) } }
                .catch { _state.value = UiState.Error(it) }
                .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
                .collect { _state.value = UiState.Results(it) }
        }
    }
    fun onQuery(q: String) { query.value = q; _state.value = UiState.Loading }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find the four bugs and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Spots one issue (maybe flatMapMerge) and says "add a try/catch". Misses the interplay between catch placement and stream termination.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is api.search a suspend function that does network on its own dispatcher? Does it throw IOException? Is the repeated same query expected to re-fire? Which thread is api.search safe on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; priority is the wrong-thread crash. If hotfixing: ensure all state writes happen on main (move collect writes via viewModelScope default Main.immediate), which is already true; see root cause below.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (the four bugs): (1) flatMapMerge instead of flatMapLatest: old responses can arrive after new ones. (2) StateFlow equality-conflation: setting query.value = q with the same value is ignored, so no new emission, while Loading was set and nothing resets it. (3) catch placed after flatMapMerge terminates the whole upstream collection; the flow is done after the first exception, so later queries do nothing. (4) The thread crash: .catch { ... } sits upstream of flowOn(IO), so its lambda runs on IO, unlike Rx where observeOn(main) was downstream of everything. Writing MutableStateFlow.value is thread-safe, but in the real app that lambda also called a UI helper (for example a toast or LiveData.setValue, which asserts main thread), hence CalledFromWrongThreadException. Also the Loading write in onQuery is racy against results arriving from the stream. Rule: flowOn changes the context of everything above it, including catch/onEach.
  4. How I'd verify each: Write runTest with fake API with controlled delays to reproduce out-of-order responses (1); test same-query retry (2); fake API throwing once then succeeding, assert second query works (3); StrictMode/thread name assertions with the debug flag on to log Thread.currentThread().name inside catch (4).
  5. Root cause: Each is a semantic mismatch: Rx switchMap cancels stale, BehaviorSubject emits repeats, onErrorReturn inside the inner stream keeps the outer alive, observeOn(main) is downstream while flowOn is upstream-only.
  6. Fix:
init {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        retryTrigger                       // MutableSharedFlow<Unit>(extraBufferCapacity = 1)
            .onStart { emit(Unit) }
            .combine(query.debounce(300)) { _, q -> q }
            .flatMapLatest { q ->
                flow {
                    emit(UiState.Loading)
                    emit(UiState.Results(api.search(q)))
                }.catch { e ->
                    if (e is CancellationException) throw e
                    emit(UiState.Error(e))
                }
            }
            .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)           // only the network part moves
            .collect { _state.value = it }    // runs on Main.immediate
    }
}

Key points: flatMapLatest; catch inside the inner flow so the outer survives; loading emitted from the stream so it can't desync; same-query retry via an explicit trigger, not StateFlow equality. 7. Prevention: Operator mapping checklist for ports; tests for stale response, same-input retry, and error recovery; lint to forbid mutating state in catch/onEach upstream of flowOn. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not catching around the whole collect; not using MutableSharedFlow(replay=1) as a blind BehaviorSubject replacement.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Where does debounce stand with flatMapLatest and cancellation of in-flight searches? → New queries cancel the in-flight inner flow; api.search must be cancellable (suspend with OkHttp Call.await).
  • Should errors be state or events? → State for persistent error UI, one-shot event channel only for transient toasts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a port that "compiled and looked identical" shipped a stale-results bug that appeared only on slow networks, never in dev; a controlled-delay test would have found it in minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: finds one bug, adds try/catch.
  • Hire: finds flatMapLatest and catch placement.
  • Strong hire: finds all four, explains mechanisms, writes reproducing tests, fixes with state-in-stream design.

questions.contextHtml:
A booking app (300k DAU) gets reports: "the confirm button spins forever" on roughly 0.8% of confirmations, reproducible in QA about 1 in 30 times on Android 12 devices. No crash, no ANR, no error log. The code path:

class BookingVM(private val repo: BookingRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val lock = Mutex()
    fun confirm() = viewModelScope.launch {
        _loading.value = true
        lock.withLock {
            val token = repo.fetchPaymentToken()      // suspend, wraps SDK callback
            repo.book(token)
        }
        _loading.value = false
    }
}
// SDK wrapper
suspend fun fetchPaymentToken(): String = suspendCoroutine { c ->
    sdk.requestToken(object : TokenListener {
        override fun onToken(t: String) = c.resume(t)
        override fun onFailure(e: Exception) = c.resumeWithException(e)
    })
}

Logs show nothing after "confirm start". The payments SDK is closed-source; its callbacks are documented as "may not fire if the app is backgrounded during init".
questions.promptHtml: How do you find out where it hangs, what's the root cause, and how do you fix it and detect it next time?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a timeout of 30 seconds." That treats the symptom, leaves the Mutex held, and loses the diagnosis.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the spinner stuck forever or until restart? Do subsequent taps also hang (suggests the lock is held)? Is it correlated with backgrounding? Does the SDK document callback guarantees?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side/idempotent booking so retry is safe; ship a client timeout plus a "try again" UI to unblock users; keep it as a stopgap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SDK callback never fires, continuation never resumed; (b) callback fires twice or after cancellation, ignored; (c) Mutex held by an earlier hung coroutine so later taps queue forever; (d) red herring: dispatcher starvation, since nothing is blocked on a thread (no ANR).
  4. How I'd verify each: Debug build with debug mode on, then the Android Studio Coroutines tab or in a JVM repro test a DebugProbes dump: expect a coroutine SUSPENDED in fetchPaymentToken and others SUSPENDED on Mutex.lock. Add CoroutineName("confirm"), log entry/exit with thread names. In QA, background the app during SDK init to reproduce, using a fake SDK that drops the callback.
  5. Root cause: suspendCoroutine waits forever when the SDK never calls back; the Mutex is held across the suspension, so every later confirm queues behind it. No thread is blocked, so no ANR, no log.
  6. Fix: Short-term: wrap with withTimeout(15_000), use suspendCancellableCoroutine with invokeOnCancellation { sdk.cancel() }, and move _loading.value = false to finally:
fun confirm() = viewModelScope.launch {
    _loading.value = true
    try {
        lock.withLock {
            val token = withTimeout(15_000) { repo.fetchPaymentToken() }
            repo.book(token)
        }
    } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) { _error.value = Retryable }
    finally { _loading.value = false }
}

Long-term: don't hold the Mutex across third-party calls; rather prevent double-submit with a state flag; ask vendor for a guaranteed callback or use their lifecycle API. 7. Prevention: Rule: every wrapper of an external callback has a timeout and cancellation; a debug-menu "live coroutines" view; @CoroutinesTimeout test with a callback that never fires. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A timeout shorter than real payment latency causes double charges, so tie it to idempotency keys. Not retrying book blindly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Timeout fires but SDK later calls back. → Resume on a cancelled continuation is ignored; make the SDK call idempotent and cancel it.
  • Why no ANR? → Suspension frees the thread; hangs from missing resumption are silent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: the dump showed 11 coroutines suspended on one Mutex whose owner awaited a callback that was lost during an OS-level process freeze; a timeout plus idempotency key closed the incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random timeout, no diagnosis.
  • Hire: identifies unresumed continuation and held Mutex.
  • Strong hire: uses coroutine dump tooling, fixes cancellation and finally, idempotency, prevention.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review of an ANR spike: ANR rate on a news app (2M DAU) jumped from 0.25% to 1.1% after release 9.3, concentrated on Android 10-12 low-end devices. Play Console ANR clusters show main thread in Object.wait inside kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking from runBlocking. Another thread dump shows all 64 DefaultDispatcher-worker-N threads in SocketInputStream.read. The release introduced a "prefetch next 30 articles" feature using Dispatchers.IO and a legacy synchronous ImageLoader.loadBlocking() called inside runBlocking from an old ContentProvider. Timeline: rollout began Tuesday, ANR alerts Wednesday, rollback Thursday.
questions.promptHtml: Run the review: what happened mechanically, what tooling would have caught it earlier, and what are the action items?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "A developer used runBlocking by mistake; tell them not to." That is blame, no systemic causes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What did the detection look like (alert thresholds, rollout stage)? Why did prefetch use the shared IO pool? How many concurrent prefetches (30 articles × images)? Was the ContentProvider call on the main thread? Did canary include low-end devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation (what was done / should be): Halt rollout at first alert, flag off prefetch remotely, then rollback. Our detection-to-action was 24 h; target under 2 h at 5 percent rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (for review): (a) IO pool exhaustion: 30 prefetch tasks × blocking reads saturate 64 threads, queueing everything else that needs IO; (b) main thread runBlocking waits on IO work stuck behind them: classic starvation deadlock-by-queueing; (c) low-end devices slower networks, longer holds; (d) red herring: coroutine count.
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dump from an ANR trace shows 64 workers blocked in socket read (a); main in joinBlocking (b). Reproduce in a JVM test with Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1)-like constrained dispatcher and fake blocking calls; Perfetto trace for thread states (Sleeping/Running vs Runnable); debug flag naming threads @prefetch#NN to attribute worker threads to the feature.
  5. Root cause: Blocking I/O occupied all IO workers; runBlocking on the main thread needed an IO worker to make progress; classic bounded-pool starvation across features sharing one pool.
  6. Fix: Short-term: cap prefetch with Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4) and use a cancellable network client (OkHttp Call.await) rather than blocking reads; remove runBlocking from the provider (use ContentProvider on a background thread with explicit timeouts or pre-populated cache). Long-term:
class Prefetcher(@PrefetchDispatcher private val d: CoroutineDispatcher /* IO.limitedParallelism(4) */) {
    suspend fun prefetch(urls: List<String>) = coroutineScope {
        val sem = Semaphore(3)
        urls.map { u -> async(d + CoroutineName("prefetch")) { sem.withPermit { loader.load(u) } } }.awaitAll()
    }
}
  1. Prevention (action items): Lint/detekt rule banning runBlocking outside tests and entry points; StrictMode detectAll in debug; CI ANR-proxy test (macrobenchmark with main-thread jank gating); canary on low-end device cohort with auto-halt on ANR delta over 0.3 points; dispatcher injection with per-feature budgets; named coroutines and a debug-flag-enabled QA build.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising the IO pool size (hides contention, raises memory). Not dropping prefetch entirely; bound it and make it lower priority (also WorkManager when idle).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does limitedParallelism not create threads? → It's a view on the parent's threads limiting concurrency; no starvation of the parent beyond its cap.
  • The ContentProvider must be synchronous. → Serve from a prepared cache; trigger refresh asynchronously; never wait on pool-bound work from Main.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: three unrelated features shared the IO pool; the one that ended up in the ANR trace was not the one that caused it, and thread names with coroutine names from a debug build were the only way to find the culprit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames a developer; no system fix.
  • Hire: diagnoses pool starvation plus runBlocking; bounds concurrency.
  • Strong hire: complete review with timeline, detection gap, tooling (thread names, Perfetto, StrictMode), preventive lint and rollout gates, and trade-offs.
